nodes.title: TAXONOMY
nodes.body:
Scientific Name: Sciaenops ocellatus
Common Name: Red Drum

nodes.title: Classification
nodes.body:
Phylum: Chordata
      Class:	Osteichthyes
      Order:  Perciformes
      Family: Sciaenidae

Other Common Names:  red fish, channel bass, drum, branded drum, spotted bass, spottail (47 80 161 327 530 543 664 784), puppy drum (834), reds (664).

nodes.title: VALUE & STATUS
nodes.body:
Commercial: Highly prized as a food fish throughout its range and is probably the most important sciaenid commercially.  Although some commercial fishery exists on the Atlantic coast, the main industry was along the northern Gulf of Mexico in Texas, Louisiana, and Florida (34 47 59 327 447 549 742).  Commercially harvested fish are mainly captured by netting using both gill and trammel nets, and also by trotlines (5 290 444 447).  Fish in the Gulf of Mexico are also caught by hand lines, beach seines in the surf, and intertidally in Gulf shrimp trawls.  Harvest occurs mainly during fall (October  December) and spring (March  June), usually in estuaries (444 791).  Florida landings statewide in 1987 were 295,157 lbs with an estimated value of $311,102, of these, 251,917 lbs were landed at ports on the west coast of Florida (902).

Decline of landings has been reported in recent years for Gulf coast states supposedly due to overfishing and habitat destruction (697 291).  These reported declines resulted in severe limiting of the harvest in Florida.

Currently, red drum are under gamefish status in Florida (There is no commercial fishing or selling allowed).

Recreational: Highly prized as both a game and food fish.  Their fighting ability on light tackle and delectable taste has probably made this fish the most important recreational species of sciaenid.  It is especially esteemed for the table in the south, but in the northern part of its range its principal interest to sportsmen is as a game fish for surf fishing (5 19 34 59 327 444 529 549).  In Florida there is a one fish limit and the length (TL) must be between 18 and 27 inches.


The most sought after fish are those less than 2.2 kg, larger fish being unpopular due to presence of parasites in the flesh and the belief that larger fish have a poor taste (5 47 59).  Fishing is primarily by rod and reel, or pole and line in surf, island passes, and estuaries especially during seasonal runs in the spring and fall (47 59 224 444).  Red drum were the primary target species of 15% of the fishermen where a target species was indicated in a recent creel census of Sarasota Bay fisheries (1274).  They are primarily caught in the fall and winter on the Florida west coast (664), but are caught yearround on the Florida Atlantic coast (1059).  In the Everglades National Park, 96% of the red drum caught were taken by recreational fishermen, producing an average annual harvest of 105,370 kg from 1972 through 1977 (1275).


Ecological Role: Marine, littoral, crepuscular predators that indiscriminately feed on the bottom or in the water column usually in shallow water (47 59 255 337 653 754 786).

Indicator: A study funded by the University of Florida has found evidence that metal poisoning has occurred among large (718 kg) red drum (96).

nodes.title: GEOGRAPHIC RANGE
nodes.body:
Overall:  Found from Massachusetts to northern Mexico including south Florida and throughout the Gulf of Mexico (788 791).  Not regularly taken in any numbers north of Chesapeake Bay and considered a straggler as far north as Massachusetts (312 784 834).

Within the study area: Common on the west coast of Florida (664 784) and Indian River Lagoon (993), and found throughout Florida waters (312 788 791 834 1059).

Mobility and Migration:

nodes.title: Life Mode
nodes.body:
Eggs, larvae, and early juveniles: are planktonic and pelagic (70 557 754).
Larvae: In the north central Gulf of Mexico, larvae were found to be vertically stratified both offshore and nearshore, with larvae being concentrated higher in the water column during the daytime than at night (1336).  This stratification did not appear to be related to larval size, temperature or salinity profiles, or microzooplankton prey distribution.
Juveniles and adults:  are pelagic and nektonic (47 70 334 526 557 754).  Juveniles larger than 70 cm are often found in schools (543), but adults are largely solitary when living in shallow water (5 47 70 116 526 529 543 557 653).  Large schools can contain 150,000 to 200,000 individuals and first appear about April and disappear offshore from September to October (529 549).  Activity seems to be equally divided between night and day (47 476 557 786).

Mobility and Migration: Relatively nonmigratory with no significant movements, but does have broad random movements, loosely coordinated temperature induced migrations, and strong offshore or deep water spawning migrations (5 481 526 549 653 754).


Eggs, larvae, and early juveniles are carried by tides and currents into the shallow estuaries and bays in late fall with peaks occurring in October.  Red drum larvae exhibit a stratified vertical distribution in both offshore and nearshore locations with larvae being concentrated higher in the water column during the day than at night (1336). This vertical distribution implies a nocturnal descent in the water column termed ‘reverse diel vertical migration’, and does not appear to be related to larval size, prey concentrations, or temperature and salinity profiles (1336).  Larvae tend to move through barrier island passes in midchannel surface waters with the tidal current (34 47 334 379 543).  Fish move from bay shores farther into the estuary to quiet back water areas as they grow, eventually occupying secondary bays considerable distances from their original point of entry (549 557 784).  Young drum will leave these shallow areas when ca. 40120 mm or 85100 mm TL and move into primary bays and somewhat deeper waters (>1.8 m).  This movement may be accelerated by cold (526 543 557 784).  Movement of subadults (<3 years) in bays appears limited, with schools remaining in a single locale for several months (526).
Most movements by this group apparently consist of responses to temperature and salinity, and foraging which can be considerable even if the fish remain within a small general area (529 535).
As juveniles approach 200 mm TL during their first spring, they may remain in deep water areas of bays or congregate near passes usually occurring in large aggregations (557 654).  Subadults may remain in the bays yearround, but older fish move out into the open Gulf in fall and winter, and possibly during late summer (553 549 292 445).  This seasonal movement is a general gradual one with fish disappearing offshore presumably to spawn (47).

nodes.title: Habitat Type
nodes.body:
Eggs and larvae: Eggs are spawned in nearshore waters close to barrier island passes and channels where larvae and postlarvae are carried by tidal currents into the shallow inside waters of bays and estuaries (47 289 334 543 557 784).  Larvae move through the passes and tend to seek shallow, slack water along the sides of the channels to prevent being carried offshore during periods of ebb tide (379 337 529 543 549 653 754 784). A study conducted in Tampa Bay found most red drum larvae in the lower portions of the bay and described an increase in larval size with distance from the bay mouth (557).  Older larvae and post larvae are euryhaline (21 152 334 529 549 557 742 754 784).


Juveniles: Euryhaline, found in a wide variety of habitats (47 152 151 161 261 334 549 557 651 653 784).  Juveniles spend the first 4 or 5 years of their lives in estuaries (543).  Move from bay shores to quiet backwater areas where 98% of juveniles occurred in Tampa Bay (85% from Alafia River alone) (557).  As they grow and begin to disperse through the bay (557). The young seek out quiet coves and lagoons rather than rough waters (543).  Older juveniles tend to move into slightly deeper, more open waters and into primary bays (47 70 526 116 152 334 529 535 543 549 559 557 653 582 651 694 754 784 786).

Adult: Euryhaline (47 152 161 261 334 653). Occasionally found in shallow bays, but tend to spend more time in marine habitats after their first spawning.  They are typically found in the Gulf of Mexico in littoral and shallow nearshore waters off beaches (47 529 535 543 549 609 754).  Often caught in more offshore waters as far as 25 km from shore in depths up to 40 m, and are commonly reported from depths of 40 to 70 m; occasionally caught on Gulf reefs (423 289 47 529 609).

nodes.title: Substrate
nodes.body:
Larvae/early juveniles: Newly hatched larvae are found in the Gulf surf over pure sand bottoms, but prefer muddy bottoms after entering bays and estuaries.  Occur there over substrates of mud, sand, or sandy mud bottoms as well as in and among patchy sea grass meadows.  The young prefer shallow tidal flats and quiet grassy areas (543).  Small juveniles seem to prefer mediumsoftmud to firm sandy substrates (559 653 784 549 754 47 337 529).  Normally associated with such sea grasses Halodule wrightii, Halodule beaudettes, Ruppia maritima, and Thallasia testudinum (786 549).

Large juveniles/adults: Common over muddy, sandy, or oyster reef bottoms with little or no sea grass (529 543 784 549).

nodes.title: Temperature
nodes.body:
Eggs/larvae: Eggs and newly hatched larvae tend to be stenothermal while 10 day and older larvae are more eurythermal (152 334 408 529).  Larvae and postlarvae have been collected in the wild from 18.3 to 31.0 C (557 549 784).

Juveniles: Eurythermal, found in waters ranging in temperature from 2.0 to 34.9 C (255 653 784 224 550 116 561 709 58 31 5 549 334 161 557).  Appear to prefer temperatures ranging from 10 to 30 (754).  Juveniles in one Tampa Bay study were collected at temperatures from 10.0 to 27.5 C (664), and 98% of the juveniles in another Tampa Bay were taken at temperatures between 12.5 and 32.2 C (557). In Charlotte Harbor, FL, juveniles found at 17.0 C (789).  Juveniles in heated discharge waters have survived up to 35 C, but at 39 C some died apparently from handling stress (529).  Large numbers have been reported killed in sudden severe cold spells, but normally fish will move into deeper waters during periods of extreme temperatures (5 653 1068).

Adults: Eurythermal, collected over a temperature range from 2.0 to 33 C (372 161 549 653 754 784).  Adults considered more susceptible to the effects of winter cold waves than smaller fish (253 784) and were among the species listed as killed by ‘freezes’ at Sanibel Island (1068); they normally move into deeper waters for refuge (653).  Red drum were not among the species in a hypothermal mortality in the Indian River Lagoon (236).

nodes.title: Salinity
nodes.body:
Eggs: Reported best salinities for 24 h survival and hatch are 30 ppt at 25 C and 34 to 36.5 ppt at 23 to 26 C (408 505 529).  Viable red drum eggs were collected in the Mosquito Lagoon and at Ponce de Leon Inlet on the Fl east coast at salinities of 29 to 32 ppt (1279), which overlaps with the ‘ideal’ range of 2530 ppt given by Holt et al (336).

Larvae:  One article reports tolerance from <1 to 50 ppt and a preference of 20 to 40 ppt salinity (754).  Larvae and postlarvae are collected in the wild were found in a salinity range of 16 to 36.4 ppt (557 784).  Spawning has occurred during salinity ranges of 14.7 to 18.5 ppt (292), 29 to 32 ppt. (1279), and ?? to ??? (1272).

Juveniles/adults: Euryhaline (47 152 161 261 334 549 653 784).  They have been collected in salinities ranging from 5.0 to 34.5 ppt in Tampa Bay (664).  Very efficient osmoregulators with the ability to tolerate abrupt changes in salinity which is especially important to juveniles in the estuarine environment.  Juveniles appear more tolerant to low salinity, whereas adults that are less dependent on estuarine areas and spend more time at sea are more tolerant of high salinity (151 784).  Collected from a salinity range of 0 to 45 ppt (0 to 34 ppt in Tampa Bay (557)), but only rarely at 50 ppt or above (152 31 58 116 161 224 255 334 372 550 549 651 653 709 754 784).  Juveniles and adults appear to prefer salinities from 20 to 40 ppt with maximum growth for juveniles occurring at 35 ppt (58 549 754 152 334 47 559).  One study found that small juveniles (1758 mm TL) were most abundant in salinities below 15 ppt.  Young and adults commonly enter Everglades rivers into freshwater, and both are likely to occur in most rivers along the coast of south Florida (265 378 790).

nodes.title: Other
nodes.body:
Oxygen: Fry can not survive low D.O.'s of 0.61.8 ppm (529).  Large juveniles have been reported in waters with D.O.'s of 5.2 to 8.4 ppm (31).

NH3: The maximum concentration allowing normal growth of larvae was 0.11 mg/liter, but older fish were found able to tolerate higher concentrations (333).

nodes.title: REPRODUCTION
nodes.body:
Mode: Oviparous, external fertilization, sexes separate.

Mating/Spawning: Onset and duration vary with photoperiod, water temperature, and possibly other factors (334 529), but typically lasts from summer through early winter.  Spawning can start as early as August in some parts of the study area, but it may extend from September to early January with peaks occurring from midAugust through October and then declining (784 59 116 289 614 549 543 334 47 529 408 292 559 445 1326).  Occurs in nearshore coastal waters on the Gulf side of barrier islands usually in or near passes and channels between islands where currents can carry eggs to shallow inside waters (70 784 614 549 334 354 47 408 292 445 557).  Spawning has also been shown to occur within estuaries such as Mosquito Lagoon on the FL east coast, and may occur within other estuaries as well (1279 1320).  Gilmore (1272) has collected red drum spawning sounds from the northern portions of the Banana River.  Spawning activities are initiated in early evening or night (246 334 529) in an average salinity of 28 ppt at an average winter temperature of 24.3 C (340).  The males are soniferous (1272) and spawning occurs from dusk until about 3 hr after dark (1327).  Spawning is concentrated around times of full and new moon (557 1279).

Fecundity: Mercer (1059) presented a table summarizing red drum fecundity estimates from both wildcaught and laboratory conditioned females.  These estimates ranged from 2.1 x 10^6 to 6.0 x 10^7 eggs per female.  Multiple spawning has been reported in laboratoryinduced spawning experiments (21).  The following lengthfecundity relationship for 22 red drum (294800mm) from Mississippi was presented by Overstreet (529):

[eq]
     Log F = 3.6976 + 0.0050(SL),   r = 0.9539
[/eq]
Where, F equals number of oocytes 16300 microns, and SL is in mm.

nodes.title: Length Range
nodes.body:
Egg: Spherical, mean diameter of 0.95 mm and a range of 0.860.98 mm diameter and buoyant (336 742).  Eggs spawned at 24 C and 28 ppt hatch in 1920 h (21), 22 h when spawned at 23 C and 36 ppt (742), and 2829 h at 2223 C (336).

Larvae: Fish less than 8.0 mm SL with those being 815 mm SL are considered transitional juveniles (557). Temperature has a pronounced effect on larval growth (336 408).  The yolksac stage can range from 40 h at 30 C to 85 h at 20 C (334 408).  Growth of laboratoryreared larvae was suggested to be 0.5mm/day (1328).  A somewhat faster growth rate has been described for wildcaught larvae (557).

Juvenile: 8.0 mm SL to ca. 40 mm TL (557). Growth tends to be sporadic in juveniles averaging 18.8 mm TL/mo or 20.4 mm SL/mo for the first 7.5 mo of life (34).  Pearson (543) reported rapid growth during the first two years with fish reaching a mean length of 33.7 cm at the end of the first year, 43.6 cm after 1.5 years, and about 64 cm by the end of the second year.  Based on counts of daily otolith rings, the following equations best described growth of 10 to 300mm juveniles (n=102) for sizeatage and ageatsize (557):

[eq]
     L = 7.1937 + 0.6320(A) + 0.0006(A^2)      r^2 = 0.98
[/eq]

and

[eq]
     A = 13.5317 + 1.4664(L)  0.0012 (L^2)     r^2 = 0.98
[/eq]

Where L equals notochord or standard length in mm, and A equals age in days.

Sexual maturity occurs at the end of the third, fourth, or fifth year with 5 year old fish constituting the bulk of the spawning population.  Males reach maturation during their third year and females mature in their fourth or fifth year (47 363 543 653).   In a cage experiment, Nadue ( ) found no growth difference in juvenile red drum grown over seagrass and over sand.


Adult: Average adult size is 800850 mm SL (468) and about 4.5 kg (834).  These are long lived fish surviving over eight years (363).  Murphy and Taylor (1326) presented both weightlength and lengthlength regressions foe adult red drum  in Florida.  They also provided lengthatage equations for red drum from both the Atlantic and Gulf coasts of Florida (1326).  Largest recorded fish is 1520 mm TL.  Robins et al (788) reported a maximum size of 1.3 m and 42 kg.

nodes.title: FOOD HABITS
nodes.body: Diet consists of food items belonging to five major groups: copepods, mysid shrimp, amphipods, decapods, and fish (34 543 70 255 651 664).  Utilization of these groups is determined by their size and availability (34 59 530).  Peters and McMicheal (557) found 85% of larvae stomachs empty, however those with food contained primarily copepods.  Small juveniles fed on mysids, amphipods and shrimp, whereas larger juveniles feed on crabs and fish.

nodes.title: ECOLOGICAL INTERACTIONS
nodes.body: Several organisms are known to parasitize red drum possibly as a consequence of the diverse foods consumed (529 549 784).

sections.heading: HEADER
sections.content:
Title: Red drum (Sciaenops ocellatus)

FLELMR Code: 1735

sections.heading: Revisions
sections.content:
05/25/93. T. Duane Phillips; Mote Marine Laboratory

Other: Added citations P. Rubec  12-18-08 from FLELMR output

sections.heading: TAXONOMY
sections.content:
Scientific Name: Sciaenops ocellatus
Common Name: Red Drum

sections.heading: Classification
sections.content:
Phylum: Chordata
      Class:	Osteichthyes
      Order:  Perciformes
      Family: Sciaenidae

Other Common Names:  red fish, channel bass, drum, branded drum, spotted bass, spottail (47 80 161 327 530 543 664 784), puppy drum (834), reds (664).

sections.heading: VALUE & STATUS
sections.content:
Commercial: Highly prized as a food fish throughout its range and is probably the most important sciaenid commercially.  Although some commercial fishery exists on the Atlantic coast, the main industry was along the northern Gulf of Mexico in Texas, Louisiana, and Florida (34 47 59 327 447 549 742).  Commercially harvested fish are mainly captured by netting using both gill and trammel nets, and also by trotlines (5 290 444 447).  Fish in the Gulf of Mexico are also caught by hand lines, beach seines in the surf, and intertidally in Gulf shrimp trawls.  Harvest occurs mainly during fall (October  December) and spring (March  June), usually in estuaries (444 791).  Florida landings statewide in 1987 were 295,157 lbs with an estimated value of $311,102, of these, 251,917 lbs were landed at ports on the west coast of Florida (902).

Decline of landings has been reported in recent years for Gulf coast states supposedly due to overfishing and habitat destruction (697 291).  These reported declines resulted in severe limiting of the harvest in Florida.

Currently, red drum are under gamefish status in Florida (There is no commercial fishing or selling allowed).

Recreational: Highly prized as both a game and food fish.  Their fighting ability on light tackle and delectable taste has probably made this fish the most important recreational species of sciaenid.  It is especially esteemed for the table in the south, but in the northern part of its range its principal interest to sportsmen is as a game fish for surf fishing (5 19 34 59 327 444 529 549).  In Florida there is a one fish limit and the length (TL) must be between 18 and 27 inches.


The most sought after fish are those less than 2.2 kg, larger fish being unpopular due to presence of parasites in the flesh and the belief that larger fish have a poor taste (5 47 59).  Fishing is primarily by rod and reel, or pole and line in surf, island passes, and estuaries especially during seasonal runs in the spring and fall (47 59 224 444).  Red drum were the primary target species of 15% of the fishermen where a target species was indicated in a recent creel census of Sarasota Bay fisheries (1274).  They are primarily caught in the fall and winter on the Florida west coast (664), but are caught yearround on the Florida Atlantic coast (1059).  In the Everglades National Park, 96% of the red drum caught were taken by recreational fishermen, producing an average annual harvest of 105,370 kg from 1972 through 1977 (1275).


Ecological Role: Marine, littoral, crepuscular predators that indiscriminately feed on the bottom or in the water column usually in shallow water (47 59 255 337 653 754 786).

Indicator: A study funded by the University of Florida has found evidence that metal poisoning has occurred among large (718 kg) red drum (96).

sections.heading: GEOGRAPHIC RANGE
sections.content:
Overall:  Found from Massachusetts to northern Mexico including south Florida and throughout the Gulf of Mexico (788 791).  Not regularly taken in any numbers north of Chesapeake Bay and considered a straggler as far north as Massachusetts (312 784 834).

Within the study area: Common on the west coast of Florida (664 784) and Indian River Lagoon (993), and found throughout Florida waters (312 788 791 834 1059).

Mobility and Migration:

sections.heading: Life Mode
sections.content:
Eggs, larvae, and early juveniles: are planktonic and pelagic (70 557 754).
Larvae: In the north central Gulf of Mexico, larvae were found to be vertically stratified both offshore and nearshore, with larvae being concentrated higher in the water column during the daytime than at night (1336).  This stratification did not appear to be related to larval size, temperature or salinity profiles, or microzooplankton prey distribution.
Juveniles and adults:  are pelagic and nektonic (47 70 334 526 557 754).  Juveniles larger than 70 cm are often found in schools (543), but adults are largely solitary when living in shallow water (5 47 70 116 526 529 543 557 653).  Large schools can contain 150,000 to 200,000 individuals and first appear about April and disappear offshore from September to October (529 549).  Activity seems to be equally divided between night and day (47 476 557 786).

Mobility and Migration: Relatively nonmigratory with no significant movements, but does have broad random movements, loosely coordinated temperature induced migrations, and strong offshore or deep water spawning migrations (5 481 526 549 653 754).


Eggs, larvae, and early juveniles are carried by tides and currents into the shallow estuaries and bays in late fall with peaks occurring in October.  Red drum larvae exhibit a stratified vertical distribution in both offshore and nearshore locations with larvae being concentrated higher in the water column during the day than at night (1336). This vertical distribution implies a nocturnal descent in the water column termed ‘reverse diel vertical migration’, and does not appear to be related to larval size, prey concentrations, or temperature and salinity profiles (1336).  Larvae tend to move through barrier island passes in midchannel surface waters with the tidal current (34 47 334 379 543).  Fish move from bay shores farther into the estuary to quiet back water areas as they grow, eventually occupying secondary bays considerable distances from their original point of entry (549 557 784).  Young drum will leave these shallow areas when ca. 40120 mm or 85100 mm TL and move into primary bays and somewhat deeper waters (>1.8 m).  This movement may be accelerated by cold (526 543 557 784).  Movement of subadults (<3 years) in bays appears limited, with schools remaining in a single locale for several months (526).
Most movements by this group apparently consist of responses to temperature and salinity, and foraging which can be considerable even if the fish remain within a small general area (529 535).
As juveniles approach 200 mm TL during their first spring, they may remain in deep water areas of bays or congregate near passes usually occurring in large aggregations (557 654).  Subadults may remain in the bays yearround, but older fish move out into the open Gulf in fall and winter, and possibly during late summer (553 549 292 445).  This seasonal movement is a general gradual one with fish disappearing offshore presumably to spawn (47).

sections.heading: Habitat Type
sections.content:
Eggs and larvae: Eggs are spawned in nearshore waters close to barrier island passes and channels where larvae and postlarvae are carried by tidal currents into the shallow inside waters of bays and estuaries (47 289 334 543 557 784).  Larvae move through the passes and tend to seek shallow, slack water along the sides of the channels to prevent being carried offshore during periods of ebb tide (379 337 529 543 549 653 754 784). A study conducted in Tampa Bay found most red drum larvae in the lower portions of the bay and described an increase in larval size with distance from the bay mouth (557).  Older larvae and post larvae are euryhaline (21 152 334 529 549 557 742 754 784).


Juveniles: Euryhaline, found in a wide variety of habitats (47 152 151 161 261 334 549 557 651 653 784).  Juveniles spend the first 4 or 5 years of their lives in estuaries (543).  Move from bay shores to quiet backwater areas where 98% of juveniles occurred in Tampa Bay (85% from Alafia River alone) (557).  As they grow and begin to disperse through the bay (557). The young seek out quiet coves and lagoons rather than rough waters (543).  Older juveniles tend to move into slightly deeper, more open waters and into primary bays (47 70 526 116 152 334 529 535 543 549 559 557 653 582 651 694 754 784 786).

Adult: Euryhaline (47 152 161 261 334 653). Occasionally found in shallow bays, but tend to spend more time in marine habitats after their first spawning.  They are typically found in the Gulf of Mexico in littoral and shallow nearshore waters off beaches (47 529 535 543 549 609 754).  Often caught in more offshore waters as far as 25 km from shore in depths up to 40 m, and are commonly reported from depths of 40 to 70 m; occasionally caught on Gulf reefs (423 289 47 529 609).

sections.heading: Substrate
sections.content:
Larvae/early juveniles: Newly hatched larvae are found in the Gulf surf over pure sand bottoms, but prefer muddy bottoms after entering bays and estuaries.  Occur there over substrates of mud, sand, or sandy mud bottoms as well as in and among patchy sea grass meadows.  The young prefer shallow tidal flats and quiet grassy areas (543).  Small juveniles seem to prefer mediumsoftmud to firm sandy substrates (559 653 784 549 754 47 337 529).  Normally associated with such sea grasses Halodule wrightii, Halodule beaudettes, Ruppia maritima, and Thallasia testudinum (786 549).

Large juveniles/adults: Common over muddy, sandy, or oyster reef bottoms with little or no sea grass (529 543 784 549).

sections.heading: Temperature
sections.content:
Eggs/larvae: Eggs and newly hatched larvae tend to be stenothermal while 10 day and older larvae are more eurythermal (152 334 408 529).  Larvae and postlarvae have been collected in the wild from 18.3 to 31.0 C (557 549 784).

Juveniles: Eurythermal, found in waters ranging in temperature from 2.0 to 34.9 C (255 653 784 224 550 116 561 709 58 31 5 549 334 161 557).  Appear to prefer temperatures ranging from 10 to 30 (754).  Juveniles in one Tampa Bay study were collected at temperatures from 10.0 to 27.5 C (664), and 98% of the juveniles in another Tampa Bay were taken at temperatures between 12.5 and 32.2 C (557). In Charlotte Harbor, FL, juveniles found at 17.0 C (789).  Juveniles in heated discharge waters have survived up to 35 C, but at 39 C some died apparently from handling stress (529).  Large numbers have been reported killed in sudden severe cold spells, but normally fish will move into deeper waters during periods of extreme temperatures (5 653 1068).

Adults: Eurythermal, collected over a temperature range from 2.0 to 33 C (372 161 549 653 754 784).  Adults considered more susceptible to the effects of winter cold waves than smaller fish (253 784) and were among the species listed as killed by ‘freezes’ at Sanibel Island (1068); they normally move into deeper waters for refuge (653).  Red drum were not among the species in a hypothermal mortality in the Indian River Lagoon (236).

sections.heading: Salinity
sections.content:
Eggs: Reported best salinities for 24 h survival and hatch are 30 ppt at 25 C and 34 to 36.5 ppt at 23 to 26 C (408 505 529).  Viable red drum eggs were collected in the Mosquito Lagoon and at Ponce de Leon Inlet on the Fl east coast at salinities of 29 to 32 ppt (1279), which overlaps with the ‘ideal’ range of 2530 ppt given by Holt et al (336).

Larvae:  One article reports tolerance from <1 to 50 ppt and a preference of 20 to 40 ppt salinity (754).  Larvae and postlarvae are collected in the wild were found in a salinity range of 16 to 36.4 ppt (557 784).  Spawning has occurred during salinity ranges of 14.7 to 18.5 ppt (292), 29 to 32 ppt. (1279), and ?? to ??? (1272).

Juveniles/adults: Euryhaline (47 152 161 261 334 549 653 784).  They have been collected in salinities ranging from 5.0 to 34.5 ppt in Tampa Bay (664).  Very efficient osmoregulators with the ability to tolerate abrupt changes in salinity which is especially important to juveniles in the estuarine environment.  Juveniles appear more tolerant to low salinity, whereas adults that are less dependent on estuarine areas and spend more time at sea are more tolerant of high salinity (151 784).  Collected from a salinity range of 0 to 45 ppt (0 to 34 ppt in Tampa Bay (557)), but only rarely at 50 ppt or above (152 31 58 116 161 224 255 334 372 550 549 651 653 709 754 784).  Juveniles and adults appear to prefer salinities from 20 to 40 ppt with maximum growth for juveniles occurring at 35 ppt (58 549 754 152 334 47 559).  One study found that small juveniles (1758 mm TL) were most abundant in salinities below 15 ppt.  Young and adults commonly enter Everglades rivers into freshwater, and both are likely to occur in most rivers along the coast of south Florida (265 378 790).

sections.heading: Other
sections.content:
Oxygen: Fry can not survive low D.O.'s of 0.61.8 ppm (529).  Large juveniles have been reported in waters with D.O.'s of 5.2 to 8.4 ppm (31).

NH3: The maximum concentration allowing normal growth of larvae was 0.11 mg/liter, but older fish were found able to tolerate higher concentrations (333).

sections.heading: REPRODUCTION
sections.content:
Mode: Oviparous, external fertilization, sexes separate.

Mating/Spawning: Onset and duration vary with photoperiod, water temperature, and possibly other factors (334 529), but typically lasts from summer through early winter.  Spawning can start as early as August in some parts of the study area, but it may extend from September to early January with peaks occurring from midAugust through October and then declining (784 59 116 289 614 549 543 334 47 529 408 292 559 445 1326).  Occurs in nearshore coastal waters on the Gulf side of barrier islands usually in or near passes and channels between islands where currents can carry eggs to shallow inside waters (70 784 614 549 334 354 47 408 292 445 557).  Spawning has also been shown to occur within estuaries such as Mosquito Lagoon on the FL east coast, and may occur within other estuaries as well (1279 1320).  Gilmore (1272) has collected red drum spawning sounds from the northern portions of the Banana River.  Spawning activities are initiated in early evening or night (246 334 529) in an average salinity of 28 ppt at an average winter temperature of 24.3 C (340).  The males are soniferous (1272) and spawning occurs from dusk until about 3 hr after dark (1327).  Spawning is concentrated around times of full and new moon (557 1279).

Fecundity: Mercer (1059) presented a table summarizing red drum fecundity estimates from both wildcaught and laboratory conditioned females.  These estimates ranged from 2.1 x 10^6 to 6.0 x 10^7 eggs per female.  Multiple spawning has been reported in laboratoryinduced spawning experiments (21).  The following lengthfecundity relationship for 22 red drum (294800mm) from Mississippi was presented by Overstreet (529):

[eq]
     Log F = 3.6976 + 0.0050(SL),   r = 0.9539
[/eq]
Where, F equals number of oocytes 16300 microns, and SL is in mm.

sections.heading: Length Range
sections.content:
Egg: Spherical, mean diameter of 0.95 mm and a range of 0.860.98 mm diameter and buoyant (336 742).  Eggs spawned at 24 C and 28 ppt hatch in 1920 h (21), 22 h when spawned at 23 C and 36 ppt (742), and 2829 h at 2223 C (336).

Larvae: Fish less than 8.0 mm SL with those being 815 mm SL are considered transitional juveniles (557). Temperature has a pronounced effect on larval growth (336 408).  The yolksac stage can range from 40 h at 30 C to 85 h at 20 C (334 408).  Growth of laboratoryreared larvae was suggested to be 0.5mm/day (1328).  A somewhat faster growth rate has been described for wildcaught larvae (557).

Juvenile: 8.0 mm SL to ca. 40 mm TL (557). Growth tends to be sporadic in juveniles averaging 18.8 mm TL/mo or 20.4 mm SL/mo for the first 7.5 mo of life (34).  Pearson (543) reported rapid growth during the first two years with fish reaching a mean length of 33.7 cm at the end of the first year, 43.6 cm after 1.5 years, and about 64 cm by the end of the second year.  Based on counts of daily otolith rings, the following equations best described growth of 10 to 300mm juveniles (n=102) for sizeatage and ageatsize (557):

[eq]
     L = 7.1937 + 0.6320(A) + 0.0006(A^2)      r^2 = 0.98
[/eq]

and

[eq]
     A = 13.5317 + 1.4664(L)  0.0012 (L^2)     r^2 = 0.98
[/eq]

Where L equals notochord or standard length in mm, and A equals age in days.

Sexual maturity occurs at the end of the third, fourth, or fifth year with 5 year old fish constituting the bulk of the spawning population.  Males reach maturation during their third year and females mature in their fourth or fifth year (47 363 543 653).   In a cage experiment, Nadue ( ) found no growth difference in juvenile red drum grown over seagrass and over sand.


Adult: Average adult size is 800850 mm SL (468) and about 4.5 kg (834).  These are long lived fish surviving over eight years (363).  Murphy and Taylor (1326) presented both weightlength and lengthlength regressions foe adult red drum  in Florida.  They also provided lengthatage equations for red drum from both the Atlantic and Gulf coasts of Florida (1326).  Largest recorded fish is 1520 mm TL.  Robins et al (788) reported a maximum size of 1.3 m and 42 kg.

sections.heading: FOOD HABITS
sections.content: Diet consists of food items belonging to five major groups: copepods, mysid shrimp, amphipods, decapods, and fish (34 543 70 255 651 664).  Utilization of these groups is determined by their size and availability (34 59 530).  Peters and McMicheal (557) found 85% of larvae stomachs empty, however those with food contained primarily copepods.  Small juveniles fed on mysids, amphipods and shrimp, whereas larger juveniles feed on crabs and fish.

sections.heading: ECOLOGICAL INTERACTIONS
sections.content: Several organisms are known to parasitize red drum possibly as a consequence of the diverse foods consumed (529 549 784).
